items.title: Suffolk brewery Adnams suffers a fall in sales after offloading some of its pubs
items.summary: Brewer and hospitality firm Adnams suffered a slowdown in sales in the first half after it put some of its pubs up for sale amid 'continued pressure' on consumer spending.
items.body:
Suffolk brewery Adnams suffers a fall in sales after offloading some of its pubs
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Brewer and hospitality firm Adnams saw sales slow in the first half after it put some of its pubs up for sale amid ‘continued pressure’ on consumer spending.
The Ghost Ship brewer said trading in its managed pubs and hotels was below expectations, with group revenue falling 8.9 per cent to £27.4million for the six months to the end of June.
It followed the disposal of some of its tenanted pubs last year as it battled ‘extremely challenging market conditions'.
The 154-year-old Suffolk brewery has come under pressure in recent years, even reportedly considering an outright sale of the business in 2024.
Adnams suffered a fall in sales after offloading some of its pubs earlier this year
An onslaught of higher costs, including higher National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage, has thwarted its turnaround efforts. The brewer ended 2025 with debts of £9.2million, down from £15.3million, but revenue was £4.3million lower than in 2024.
Chair Simon Townsend today said the business was ‘resilient despite continued pressure on consumer spending and subdued trading conditions’.
It said it cut operating expenses by over £2million in the period, which it said helped to mitigate some of the impact on overall profitability.
Adnams reported a pre-tax loss of £1.42million in the first half, compared to £1.47million in the previous year.
Pub and hotel sales started to pick up over the summer thanks to the warmer weather and World Cup, with like-for-like sales growth of 3.3 per cent in July, while profits climbed 10 per cent.
Direct-to-consumer sales proved more robust in the first half with trading in supermarkets continuing to outperform the wider beer market, as it piles money into its Ghost Ship brands.
The company added: 'Adnams today is a more focused business than it was two years ago.
'Whilst there remains much work to do, the board believes the actions being taken are the right ones to create a more resilient, profitable and sustainable business over the long term.'

items.body:
Sainsbury's Tu taps RFID and Tesco makes key AI/CX hire: this week's biggest retail technology stories
It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including M&S, Dollar General, Asda, Vusion, Whataburger, Alcampo, Hanshow, JD Sports, HyperFinity, and The Home Depot.
1. M&S claims an AI first as it deploys animal welfare monitoring tools across dairy farms
M&S says it has become the first retailer to use AI powered monitoring systems on its entire Milk Pool to monitor animal welfare across 46 dairy farms. The tools use cameras to capture footage of dairy cows when they are indoors which is then analysed using an algorithm trained alongside vets to monitor welfare of dairy cows in real-time.
The technology uses AI powered video analytics to build an individual health profile for each animal, tracking mobility and body condition scoring over time to give farmers objective, consistent data on the wellbeing of their herd. The tools monitor the cow’s behaviour including lying time, feeding time, social interactions and mobility to generate a ‘cow comfort score’ which supports vets in their assessment of individual cow’s health. The cameras will assess body condition scoring to assess cows’ nutritional status over time.
Terry Canning, CEO of Cattle Eye says “Changes in body condition are early indicators of metabolic health, fertility, and overall wellbeing. Tracking those changes more regularly, across every cow, gives farmers a level of insight that was previously unavailable outside research environments.”
The algorithm supporting the tool has been tested and, according to those involved, found to perform to the same standard as a trained welfare assessor.
The tools are being rolled out following trials at a selection of M&S dairy farms, where farmers have used the technology to make changes to tailor care to individual cow’s needs. By measuring lying times, farmers have made changes to the bedding of individual cows to improve their comfort based on their specific size and shape. Feeding schedules have been adapted to reduce the amount of time cows spend standing and the design of some stalls has been adapted to improve cow comfort.
2. RELEX Solutions announces AI powered tie up with Dollar General for forecasting and replenishment
RELEX Solutions is partnering with Dollar General to implement forecasting, replenishment, and allocation capabilities across its North American operations.
Dollar General operates more than 21,000 stores and 34 distribution centres, managing approximately 18,000 SKUs, and continues to expand its store footprint each year. The AI driven RELEX platform will manage store replenishment, ordering schedules, lead times, supplier coordination, and fulfillment methods in one place. Sales patterns and other demand factors will be built directly into the planning process, allowing DCs and stores to work from the same data.
“We chose RELEX because it gives us a practical way to use AI in our planning and helps our teams focus on the issues that truly need attention,” says Jeff Vaughan, SVP Global Inventory Management at Dollar General. “The platform brings forecasting, replenishment, and allocation planning into a single environment, giving our teams greater visibility across the network.”
3. The Home Depot has bagged the Holy Grail of omnichannel retail with its latest AI shopping assistant move
The Home Depot has announced the US wide roll-out of new in-store capabilities for Magic Apron, its Al powered shopping assistant. Customers can open it in the retailer’s mobile app or scan a QR code on in-store signage.
"Customers come to The Home Depot for expert guidance, and we know they want their shopping experience to be easy and efficient," says Jordan Broggi, EVP of Interconnected Retail. "Magic Apron takes the best of our digital expertise and brings it into the physical store, creating a more connected shopping experience that helps customers find products, get project guidance and make decisions faster. Our associates remain at the centre of the shopping experience, and Magic Apron gives customers another way to access guidance and support while they're in our stores."
This is the Holy Grail of omnichannel retail, according to Michael Guzzetta, Retail Innovation & Strategy Leader at Cookie Plug San Antonio, and a former H-E-B executive.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: “It's moments like these when an AI assistant stops being just another digital feature and starts making physical promises a reality. Customers can ask questions by text, voice, or image. Then, Magic Apron can provide project guidance, check local availability, and even point someone to a specific aisle and bay. The model is the visible part for the customer, but the harder job will be for the back end teams to keep several operating systems honest at the same time: Local inventory; Aisle and bay mapping; Product compatibility; Store specific knowledge; The handoff to an associate when the answer is incomplete or wrong.”
He added: “Anyone who has worked around store systems knows that “aisle 14, bay 6” isn’t just a helpful customer answer... It’s a promise built on receiving, stocking, planogram changes, shrink, inventory accuracy, and whatever happened on the floor ten minutes ago. Now zoom out to a nationwide scale and the important questions change."
"How quickly does local reality reach the assistant? How does an associate correct a bad answer? Who owns the recovery when the guidance is technically sound but the product isn’t actually there?”
Magic Apron is compelling because it connects advice to the physical store, Guzzetta argues. Its biggest test will be how often the store can keep the promise its digital friend just made.
4. Sainsbury's deploys RFID technology for Tu clothing range across 400 of its stores
Sainsbury's is rolling out radio frequency identification (RFID) technology across its TU clothing departments in approximately 400 stores, with the project set for completion by early September.
This follows a pilot earlier this year, which enabled the retailer to improve its stock level visibility, speed up replenishment and manage stock more efficiently.
“Really proud of my team and the role they’ve played in deploying this project across our stores. A huge amount of work, collaboration and energy behind the scenes to bring this to life,” says Gillian Ekin, Head of Transformation and Operational Development at Sainsbury’s.
RTIH has reached out to Sainsbury’s regarding specifics of the implementation, such as suppliers involved, and we will update this article when we receive a response.
5. Step change for customers and staff as Asda wraps Vusion ESELs roll-out at convenience stores
Asda has completed the roll-out of eSELs across its Asda Express petrol stations, Asda Express locations and Asda petrol station estate, with the deployment covering over 550 stores.
In a LinkedIn post, Anthony McCarron, Projects, Propostions & Comms Manager at Asda, said: "This is a massive achievement across so many internal and external stakeholders, so thank you - big shout to Daniel Pelissier for leading this project from start to finish on time and on budget."
"Our Vusion eSELs, installed by our delivery partner Renovotec, are delivering a real step change for customers and colleagues. Thank you to Elecomm, MADIC UK, and Evolve for the infrastructure support in achieving this huge milestone for our convenience stores."
6. Starbucks veteran Rob Dellinger joins Whataburger as its new Vice President of Restaurant Technology
American fast food chain Whataburger has appointed Rob Dellinger as Vice President of Restaurant Technology. He joins from Starbucks where he spent almost 26 years, most recently serving as Director PoS Application Development.
A spokesperson for Whataburger says: “Rob joins us after more than 25 years at Starbucks, where he helped modernise technology supporting more than 15,000 stores across North America. At Whataburger, he’ll lead the technology that powers our restaurants, making it simpler, stronger and more scalable for our employees and the guests we serve.”
“Rob is a seasoned innovator who has managed complex technology at scale and has the instincts to start where it matters: in the restaurant, listening to employees and understanding the work,” says Chief Digital and Technology Transformation Office Rohit Kapoor. “That combination will make him a tremendous partner as we strengthen the systems our restaurants rely on today and build for Whataburger’s continued growth.”
7. Sephora launches on TikTok Shop with pilot going live across US during September
Sephora has announced its debut on TikTok Shop. Piloting in the United States from 19th September, its Drop Shop experience will feature exclusive monthly drops, showcasing curated products from some of Sephora's most popular partner brands. Each featured brand will have a dedicated moment to bring its products to life, tell its story and connect with new audiences.
Each drop will include teasers, interactive experiences, and creator led content, encouraging consumers to guess the brand in the spotlight. The experience will culminate in an official TikTok LIVE with a celebrity host, brand founders, and creators to unveil the featured products, answer audience questions, engage with viewers in real-time, and showcase products available for purchase on TikTok Shop during the LIVE.
“Beauty discovery has always been core to Sephora’s ethos, and the rise of social commerce and digital marketplaces have reinforced the need to evolve how we engage with our beauty lovers. We already have an incredibly active beauty community on TikTok, so we are excited to take the next step and pilot the Sephora Drop Shop on TikTok Shop. This platform gives us a new way to interact with our existing customers, while extending our reach to a highly immersed beauty audience. Importantly, the launch signifies a natural progression in how we continue to lead and innovate in beauty retail,” says Artemis Patrick, President and CEO at Sephora North America.
Products featured in each monthly drop will launch exclusively through Sephora's TikTok Shop, with select items later rolling out to Sephora.com, in selected Sephora stores or through other retail partners. During the exclusive launch window, customers will still be able to preview the products on the Sephora site ahead of their wider availability.
8. JD Sports gets personal as it enlists HyperFinity to deliver actionable customer behaviour insights
HyperFinity has partnered with JD Sports to design and deliver a personalisation programme that aims to equip the retailer with a clear evidence base for its loyalty strategy.
It has designed a personalisation engine and trialled this to build a framework for JD Sports UK. The solution was trialled to prove: The value of ‘buy again’ category offers to assess how active customers respond to identify the optimal spend multiplier incentives; The optimal incentive mix for high and low spenders for cash-based rewards versus spend multipliers; The ability to drive incremental basket spend through cross-sell offers aligned to previous purchase history, testing product affinity and which category follow-ons drive incremental spend.
According to those involved, the trials established that relevance consistently outperforms simply increasing incentive value, and that higher spenders respond better to spend multipliers, while lower spenders react similarly to both. Alongside this, they identified that campaign spacing must be tailored to individual behaviour to avoid offer fatigue.
The partnership delivered a significant material impact on topline performance, including an uplift in total in-store loyalty sales across JD Sports UK during the trial period. Based on the results, JD Sports has identified a multi-million pound opportunity to grow in-store loyalty sales within the first year of scaling the programme.
In addition to the analysis, HyperFinity delivered a suite of assets, including measurement dashboards, customer segmentations, campaign templates, and product seasonality and affinity insights, enabling JD Sports to continue building on the programme.
9. Alcampo deploys Hanshow ESLs across supermarkets as part of modernisation push
Chinese firm Hanshow is working with Alcampo (Auchan Retail), a Spanish grocery retailer, on the roll-out of electronic shelf labels across 84 supermarkets.
With more than 560,000 ESLs being deployed, the initiative will help eliminate approximately 1,843 km of paper price strips annually, avoiding an estimated 8.4 tonnes of CO₂ emissions each year while supporting Alcampo's broader sustainability goals.
Beyond reducing paper consumption, ESLs provide a centralised platform for pricing and shelf-edge communication, helping ensure accurate and up-to-date product information across stores. The solution is also expected to reduce time spent on shelf-label updates and allow store teams to focus more on customer facing activities.
A spokesperson for Hanshow says: “We're delighted to partner with Alcampo as it continues to modernise store operations and advance a more sustainable retail environment.”
10. Lucy Cooper departs THG Ingenuity and takes on Group Customer Experience & Agentic Director at Tesco
Lucy Cooper has joined Tesco as Group Customer Experience & Agentic Director. She was previously at THG Ingenuity where she served as Chief Commercial Officer. In a LinkedIn post, she said: “I’ve had a brilliant time at THG. Fast, ambitious, and occasionally bonkers (but never, ever boring).”
“I’ve learned an enormous amount, always at speed and leave with huge respect for the ambition of the business and the people building it. I remain of course a loyal shareholder and fan. But now - to Tesco!”
She added: “Few businesses have a bigger place in British life, serve more people, or have quite so much opportunity to use technology and data to change how millions of customers shop. That combination was pretty difficult to resist. The most interesting question in commerce right now isn’t how AI helps people shop. It’s what happens when AI starts shopping for them. The weekly shop might be the perfect proving ground… high frequency, habitual and highly personal.”
“Full of decisions most of us would happily delegate. There are opportunities abound across the rest of the group in Tesco Mobile, banking and health, all underpinned by the OG data platform, dunnhumby. I’m thrilled to be taking on remit for the group wide response. I’m excited to get started, meet the team, and work out quite how much I don’t yet know about groceries.”

items.body:
Nick Elms leaves VolkerWessels UK as he bags Global Information Technology Director role at WHSmith
WHSmith has appointed Nick Elms as Global Information Technology Director. He joins from engineering and construction firm VolkerWessels UK where he served as Director of Information Technology. His CV also includes stints at Balfour Beatty and British Land.
ESLs
WHSmith and SOLUM recently announced a partnership involving the deployment of electronic shelf label (ESL) solutions across the retailer’s UK travel estate, starting with high footfall locations including the retailer’s recently opened flagship stores at Heathrow Airport.
To support the roll-out, WHSmith has selected Newton PRO, SOLUM’s flagship ESL designed for demanding retail environments such as airports, railway stations and major transport hubs.
Heidi Reynolds, Retail Director at WHSmith, said: “Our focus is on making every journey better by bringing together all of the essentials travellers need in one place. As we continue to evolve our offer, the ESL solutions help us support a clearer and more intuitive customer experience while enabling colleagues to operate more efficiently in busy travel environments.”
Mark Duckworth, Country Manager UK & Ireland at SOLUM, said: “WHSmith’s new flagship stores reflect the continued evolution of travel retail, where convenience, speed and clarity are essential to the customer journey. We are proud to support it with ESL solutions designed for high footfall environments, helping improve shelf-edge accuracy, operational efficiency and the in-store experience across key travel locations. This partnership is an important milestone for SOLUM as we continue to strengthen our presence in the UK travel retail market.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
ESLs will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.summary: Shopper numbers were 3.1% lower last month than in August last year following a 3.8% decline in July, according to the British Retail Consortium.
items.body:
'Too hot to shop' weather leaves High Street deserted over the summer in latest blow to retailers
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The High Street was deserted over the summer as it was deemed ‘too hot to shop’.
Shopper numbers were 3.1 per cent lower last month than in August last year, following a 3.8 per cent decline in July, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
The slump was just the latest blow to shopkeepers already battling soaring costs, higher taxes and subdued demand.
BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said: 'Retailers don't need warm words, they need lower costs.
'With his first Budget weeks away, Chancellor John Healey has a chance to throw Britain's high streets a lifeline.
'Government action on business rates and energy costs would help keep prices down, support investment, and sustain the jobs and communities that retail underpins across the country.'

items.title: Forty per cent of retailers face customer complaints despite claiming unified commerce success
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Nearly nine in ten UK retailers believe they have cracked unified commerce, but new report How UK merchants are measuring up to unified retail suggests many customers are still experiencing the consequences of disconnected systems. A study of 200 UK retail decision-makers by unified retail agency Visualsoft and Shopify found that 89% of retailers believe unified commerce is essential […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Nearly nine in ten UK retailers believe they have cracked unified commerce, but new report How UK merchants are measuring up to unified retail suggests many customers are still experiencing the consequences of disconnected systems.
A study of 200 UK retail decision-makers by unified retail agency Visualsoft and Shopify found that 89% of retailers believe unified commerce is essential to future growth and 85% say their systems enable them to deliver a consistent experience across online and in-store channels.
Yet despite that confidence, 40% have received customer complaints about inconsistent experiences, 38% have lost sales because of inaccurate inventory information and 32% have struggled to keep pricing and promotions aligned across channels.
The findings suggest that while retailers have largely won the battle to connect channels, many are still struggling to keep systems aligned in day-to-day operations.
Chris Fletcher, CEO of Visualsoft, said: “Most merchants now recognise the commercial value of unified retail and the benefits it brings to both their business and their customers. That’s a massive step in the right direction, and something we’re really pleased to see.
“However, this research also highlights that connecting systems alone doesn’t guarantee consistency. Customers expect pricing, promotions, stock and service to be consistent wherever they choose to browse and buy, and that’s where unified retail really proves its worth.”
The research found a particularly striking gap between confidence and performance when it comes to inventory. While 83% of retailers believe inventory data is accurate and visible across channels, more than a third have still lost sales because stock information was inaccurate or unavailable.
A similar pattern emerges in customer data. Although 84% say they have a clear view of customer behaviour across online and in-store journeys, a third admit they have experienced limited visibility because of disconnected systems.
The research also found that many retailers have focused on connecting transactions before connecting customers. Payments and checkout are now the most integrated part of the retail stack, with 81% of retailers reporting alignment across online and in-store systems. However, only 59% say customer profiles and purchase history are connected across channels.
Other areas remain surprisingly fragmented. Just 46% of retailers support gift cards consistently across online and in-store systems, while only 59% offer unified returns and 58% support ship-from-store fulfilment.
According to Visualsoft, these operational gaps are becoming increasingly important as customer expectations continue to rise.
Matthew Eley, retail project lead at Visualsoft Said: “Retailers are no longer being judged on whether they offer ecommerce, stores or omnichannel services. Those are now baseline expectations.
“The differentiator is consistency. You can have as many channels as you like but if it’s difficult for consumers to navigate them, you’ll get complaints, lose sales, and eventually customers will leave. The new suite of retail technology is enabling retailers to keep it unified.”
The challenge is particularly significant because most retailers believe they are already close to the finish line. Almost half (46%) describe their operations as fully unified across ecommerce, stores and customer data, while a further 40% say they are partially connected.
However, the operational reality suggests that integration remains a work in progress. More than half of retailers (56%) cite technology costs as a barrier to further progress, 45% identify inventory accuracy as a challenge and 42% point to integration complexity as a major constraint.
“The next phase of retail transformation isn’t about adding more channels or making things more complicated,” Matthew added. “It’s about making every channel behave as one, like consumers want.”

items.body:
The Morrisons Foundation is today launching ‘Connecting Communities’, a new £1 million fund to help local charities improve, maintain and upgrade the shared spaces at the heart of their communities.
Grants of up to £20,000 are available for charities in local communities that need financial support to improve their physical spaces. Funding is specifically targeted at capital improvements, including new equipment, essential maintenance, or refurbishments.
Charities running spaces and activities that bring people together to connect, socialise and access vital support, such as village halls, youth clubs and community centres, are encouraged to apply for a share of the £1 million fund. This also includes organisations providing place-based support in the communities, including warm hubs for the elderly, school PTAs and hospices.
David Scott, chair of the Morrisons Foundation, said: “Thriving communities are built on the strength of their shared spaces but funding to sustain them is in short supply. Our new Connecting Communities grants will breathe new life into community facilities that bring people together and provide important local services.”
Joseph Clark-Bland, Morrisons’ charity and community manager, said: “Our new Connecting Communities fund is designed to unlock the potential of local neighbourhoods facilities. We know many charities providing vital services in our communities are struggling. We want to help ensure they remain open and accessible.”
Since launching in 2015, the Morrisons Foundation has donated almost £50 million through community grants and matched the fundraising of Morrisons colleagues, supporting thousands of charities across England, Scotland and Wales.
Charities with a project that could benefit from the new Connecting Communities fund are invited to find out more and apply at morrisonsfoundation.com.

items.body:
John Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results.
The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air on YouTube with clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast.
The premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show. There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off.
Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which is forcing retailers to change their marketing plans.
The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology.
Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its ‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge.
Ruis, who departs John Lewis this weekend after almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”.
He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.
Ruis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas.
Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend.
The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said.
“It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.”
Ruis last month announced his abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”. He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry.
“We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”.
Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which was bought out of administration by Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month.
He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.

items.body:
Heritage sports and lifestyle brand New Era has signed a 10-year lease for a flagship store at 386 Oxford Street, London, with Savills acting on behalf of the private landlord.
The brand will occupy the entire corner building, comprising more than 2,500 sq ft across basement, ground and four upper floors. Located adjacent to Selfridges and close to Bond Street station, the site will provide New Era with a highly visible presence at the western end of Oxford Street.
Founded in 1920, New Era has evolved from a family-owned cap manufacturer into a globally recognised brand at the forefront of sport, fashion and culture. Best known for its iconic 59FIFTY cap and its longstanding partnerships with major US sports leagues, the brand has become a staple of both professional sport and streetwear culture worldwide.
Callum White, associate director in Retail at Savills, comments: “The momentum on Oxford Street is accelerating, with the upcoming pedestrianisation acting as a powerful magnet for global retailers. New Era’s arrival is another vote of confidence in this shifting energy, proving that top brands are eager to plant their flags ahead of a reimagined, traffic-free environment.”

items.body:
GreyOrange, the global leader in AI-powered multi-agent warehouse orchestration and store inventory software, announced today that more than 3,800 retail locations globally run on its technology. Some of the world’s largest retailers, including H&M Group, use its inventory software gStore to increase sales and improve shopper experiences.
The AI-powered gStore platform, which includes merchandising software and connects with technologies such as RFID (radio frequency identification) readers and smart mirrors, has managed approximately 200 million retail inventory items across live deployments. That represents hundreds of millions of jackets, shoes, accessories, pet supplies and more tracked and located within stores.
Deploying physical AI on the store floor
The gStore platform uses sensor-agnostic technology, including overhead or handheld RFID readers, to locate specific inventory items to within 3 to 5 feet. It connects with sales data to inform retailers which SKUs sell the fastest and which get abandoned in fitting rooms, where to place products to optimize sales, and when stock is running low. This real-time inventory “heat map” helps associates quickly replenish shelves and find items for customers.
GreyOrange operates 130,000 hardware- and software-based agents across stores and warehouses, the world’s largest heterogeneous fleet. The physical AI software provider has added 100,000 agents in the last two years as it expands its global footprint among fashion, specialty and general merchandise retailers.
“Many of the world’s largest retailers run their core operations on GreyOrange. Their scale, operational complexity, and willingness to co-develop the future of omnichannel technology rather than simply adopt it have helped us shape how our platform performs,” said Akash Gupta, Co-founder and CEO of GreyOrange. “We’ve reached this milestone of 3,800 stores live thanks to customers like H&M Group, whose deep partnership empowers us to keep building physical AI solutions that fit how busy retailers operate.”
GreyOrange in action at H&M Group
H&M Group rolled out GreyOrange’s warehouse orchestration platform GreyMatter in 2021 in one of its West Coast distribution centers, enabling new omnichannel capabilities and enhanced customer service levels. Since then, the partnership has expanded from U.S. distribution centers to a global footprint, with GreyMatter deployed across additional North American facilities and gStore implemented in hundreds of retail locations across three continents, further connecting stores and distribution centers across the network.
gStore has driven operational efficiency in H&M Group stores through better inventory management, faster replenishment and increased picking efficiency. In the distribution centers, GreyMatter has enhanced fulfillment performance by streamlining order processing, reducing operational costs and speeding up e-commerce deliveries.
“H&M Group constantly explores new technologies that improve how our customers shop and how our teams work,” said David Pino, Head of Emerging Technology at H&M. “Beyond a strong product, scaling technology across our network takes a specialized understanding of how stores, fulfillment operations and inventory flows work together to support a seamless customer experience. With GreyOrange, we’re refining store and fulfillment workflows to meet the speed, complexity and omnichannel demands of global fashion retail.”
H&M Group has launched the AI-powered inventory software in hundreds of locations with more to come.

items.title: China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott
items.summary: Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson Almost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market . Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis. Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. items.body:
Almost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market. Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.
Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.
This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.
Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.
The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles. It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.
Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products.
Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.
In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.
As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power,” says Campanella.
Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.
The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.
Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble.
Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.
There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.
The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.
- 
  Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

items.body:
Lucy Cooper departs THG Ingenuity and takes on Group Customer Experience & Agentic Director role at Tesco
Lucy Cooper has joined Tesco as Group Customer Experience & Agentic Director. She was previously at THG Ingenuity where she served as Chief Commercial Officer. In a LinkedIn post, she said: “I’ve had a brilliant time at THG. Fast, ambitious, and occasionally bonkers (but never, ever boring).”
“I’ve learned an enormous amount, always at speed and leave with huge respect for the ambition of the business and the people building it. I remain of course a loyal shareholder and fan. But now - to Tesco!”
She added: “Few businesses have a bigger place in British life, serve more people, or have quite so much opportunity to use technology and data to change how millions of customers shop. That combination was pretty difficult to resist. The most interesting question in commerce right now isn’t how AI helps people shop. It’s what happens when AI starts shopping for them. The weekly shop might be the perfect proving ground… high frequency, habitual and highly personal.”
“Full of decisions most of us would happily delegate. There are opportunities abound across the rest of the group in Tesco Mobile, banking and health, all underpinned by the OG data platform, dunnhumby. I’m thrilled to be taking on remit for the group wide response. I’m excited to get started, meet the team, and work out quite how much I don’t yet know about groceries.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
AI will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

H&M Group launches gStore in hundreds of locations as GreyOrange brings physical AI to stores
GreyOrange reports that more than 3,800 retail locations globally now run on its technology, with the likes of H&M Group using its inventory software gStore.
The AI powered platform, which includes merchandising software and connects with technologies such as RFID (radio frequency identification) readers and smart mirrors, has managed approximately 200 million retail inventory items across live deployments.
It uses sensor agnostic technology, including overhead or handheld RFID readers, to locate specific inventory items to within three to five feet. It connects with sales data to inform retailers which SKUs sell the fastest and which get abandoned in fitting rooms, where to place products to optimise sales, and when stock is running low. This real-time inventory “heat map” helps associates quickly replenish shelves and find items for customers.
“Many of the world’s largest retailers run their core operations on GreyOrange. Their scale, operational complexity, and willingness to co-develop the future of omnichannel technology rather than simply adopt it have helped us shape how our platform performs,” says Akash Gupta, Co-founder and CEO at GreyOrange. “We’ve reached this milestone of 3,800 stores live thanks to customers like H&M Group, whose deep partnership empowers us to keep building physical AI solutions that fit how busy retailers operate.”
H&M Group rolled out GreyOrange’s warehouse orchestration platform GreyMatter in 2021 in one of its West Coast distribution centres. Since then, the partnership has expanded to a global footprint, with GreyMatter deployed across additional North American facilities and gStore implemented in hundreds of retail locations across three continents.
“H&M Group constantly explores new technologies that improve how our customers shop and how our teams work,” says David Pino, Head of Emerging Technology at H&M. “Beyond a strong product, scaling technology across our network takes a specialised understanding of how stores, fulfillment operations and inventory flows work together to support a seamless customer experience. items.title: Blame Vinted, eBay and Depop: charity shops hit hard as many donors turn to popular online sellers
items.summary: Charity shops are under pressure as donors sell higher value clothes and goods through online platforms such as Vinted, eBay and Depop, rather than donating them, according to research from Rathbones, a UK charity wealth manager. Its study, involving 100 senior charity executives and 1,000 donors, found both groups are seeing fewer of the best clothes and other items reaching charity shops as more people use online resale sites. 38% of senior executives at charities which run shops say they have seen a fall in the quality of donations they receive since the rise of Vinted , eBay and Depop. Around one in ten say the drop in the quality of donations has been significant. Around 42% note that the quality of donations is unchanged while 18% are receiving better quality items. The squeeze on charity shops is also reflected in Rathbones research undertaken with people who give items to charity shops. 49% of respondents admit their use of online sellers has had an impact on what they donate.
items.body:
Blame Vinted, eBay and Depop: charity shops hit hard as many donors turn to popular online sellers
Charity shops are under pressure as donors sell higher value clothes and goods through online platforms such as Vinted, eBay and Depop, rather than donating them, according to research from Rathbones, a UK charity wealth manager.
Its study, involving 100 senior charity executives and 1,000 donors, found both groups are seeing fewer of the best clothes and other items reaching charity shops as more people use online resale sites.
38% of senior executives at charities which run shops say they have seen a fall in the quality of donations they receive since the rise of Vinted, eBay and Depop. Around one in ten say the drop in the quality of donations has been significant. Around 42% note that the quality of donations is unchanged while 18% are receiving better quality items.
The squeeze on charity shops is also reflected in Rathbones research undertaken with people who give items to charity shops. 49% of respondents admit their use of online sellers has had an impact on what they donate. 21% say there has been a slight drop in what they give as they keep their best items to sell online, while 19% admit the quality of clothes they donate is significantly lower as they only give charity shops items that do not sell. Around 9% have stopped giving to charity shops and only sell online.
Charity shops make a major contribution to charity finances - data shows the profit contribution of charity retail organisations is around £300 million a year with more than 9,900 shops employing around 24,900 employees supported by more than 223,500 volunteers.
David Cox, Director of Charities at Rathbones, says: “Charity shops are an important source of income for many charities, so any shift in the quality or volume of donated goods matters for the sector. It is understandable that people may want to sell higher-value items online, particularly while household finances remain under pressure, but this research shows there can be a knock-on effect for charity retailers.”
“The good news is that selling online and supporting charities do not have to be mutually exclusive. Donors can still give a portion of what they earn, use platform donation options where available, or continue donating items that charities can resell. Small choices can make a meaningful difference to charities that rely on retail income.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Online marketplaces will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

items.title: B&Q and Five Guys among firms that paid staff below minimum wage
items.summary: More than 600 companies underpaid staff, with £4m returned to workers, according to the government.
items.body:
B&Q and Five Guys among firms that paid staff below minimum wage
- Published
DIY store B&Q and the fast food chain Five Guys are among hundreds of UK businesses named by the government for paying staff below the minimum wage.
More than 600 employers were ordered to pay affected workers the outstanding wages, with Â£4m returned to workers, according to the Department for Business and Trade.
The firms have also been issued penalties worth Â£7m.
B&Q said the underpayments were unintentional and the result of calculations involving geographical allowances, while Five Guys blamed "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied".
The list of 658 businesses includes shops, restaurants, nurseries, social care providers and a handful of NHS trusts. The government did not say over what time period the underpayments spanned.
Minimum wage is Â£12.71 for staff aged 21 and over. For 18 to 20 year olds the rate is Â£10.85, and for under 18s and apprentices it is Â£8.
B&Q underpaid 4,530 workers a total of more than Â£456,000, according to the government.
B&Q said in response: "The shortfalls in payments were unintentional. They relate to calculations involving geographical allowances which are paid in addition to minimum hourly rates. All affected colleagues were quickly paid in full in July 2025."
Five Guys, named in the list as owing over Â£54,000 to 3,699 staff, said "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied" led to its underpayments, which were identified in a review by the HMRC, the UK's revenue and tax authority.
"We worked closely and transparently with HMRC throughout the process and have made all required payments to affected current and former employees," the company said.
St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group failed to pay over Â£123,000 to 75 workers, according to the list, which also says St George's University Hospitals in Wandsworth, London, underpaid 55 workers.
A spokesman for the two hospital trusts said that "no colleagues were underpaid".
"This relates to a technical compliance issue where part of their salary for a non tax-deductable 'salary sacrifice' (for example, towards childcare) was not counted towards the national minimum wage, even though their gross salary was above the national minimum wage," he said.
A spokesperson said apprentices at Norfolk Community Health and Care NHS Trust were inadvertently underpaid between 2019 and 2023.
They said while their pay met the requirements for their contracted hours, meetings, handovers and time spent changing into uniform hadn't been accounted for, adding the trust has since changed policies and practices.
The other trust named has been contacted for comment.
There were also several nursing homes on the list, and multiple childcare providers.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the government was determined to stamp out the practice of "short-changing your staff".
"The best businesses know that looking after your workers isn't just the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do," he said.
Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: "Underpaying your staff is illegal, and we will not let workers foot the bill for their boss failing to follow the rules."
"Every employer should check their payroll now and reach out to Acas if they need further support," she added.
The first 10 employers on the government's list, which was sorted by the amount of wages not paid, are:
1. B&Q Ltd, failed to pay Â£456,934.72 to 4,530 workers.
2. Elysium Healthcare Holdings 3 Ltd, Borehamwood, failed to pay Â£330,048.81 to 1,095 workers.
3. St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group, failed to pay Â£123,331.97 to 75 workers.
4. Support Staff Services Limited, Slough, failed to pay Â£119,715.13 to 323 workers.
5. Forest Holidays Ltd, Moira, failed to pay Â£100,308.68 to 598 workers.
6. St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London (Wandsworth), failed to pay Â£77,498.91 to 55 workers.
7. Lanes Group Limited, Leeds, failed to pay Â£67,893.34 to 297 workers.
8. UK Care Team Ltd, Leicester, LE19, failed to pay Â£67,082.76 to 99 workers.
9. Five Guys JV Limited, London (Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea), failed to pay Â£54,642.47 to 3,699 workers.
10. Merlin Cinemas Limited, Redruth, failed to pay Â£50,198.75 to 181 workers.
The list marks the first "naming round" since the Fair Work Agency was set up in April under the Employment Rights Act.
As well as enforcing the minimum wage, the agency also will soon tackle practices of denying workers holiday and sick pay.
Chair of the agency's advisory board, Matthew Taylor, said naming employers which underpay staff was an important reminder that "paying the minimum wage is not optional - it is the law".
He said: "Most employers want to do the right thing, and we will support them to comply, but those who fall short should expect robust enforcement to protect workers and maintain a fair playing field for responsible businesses."

items.title: Retailers urge Healey to unwind national insurance hike to boost jobs
items.summary: Retailers have called on Chancellor John Healey to unwind some of the national insurance reforms made by his predecessor in a bid to tackle the youth joblessness crisis.  The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which represents retailers including Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Marks & Spencer, has written to the Chancellor, urging him to unwind “soaring employment costs”.  [...]
items.body:
Retailers urge Healey to unwind national insurance hike to boost jobs
Retailers have called on Chancellor John Healey to unwind some of the national insurance reforms made by his predecessor in a bid to tackle the youth joblessness crisis.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which represents retailers including Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Marks & Spencer, has written to the Chancellor, urging him to unwind “soaring employment costs”.
At the 2024 Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves hiked the rate of employer national insurance contributions (NICs) to 15 per cent and brought the threshold at which bosses pay the tax down from £9,100 to £5,000.
The tax changes saddled retailers with more than £2.3bn in extra costs, the BRC said. Recent hikes to the national minimum wage have piled a further £4.1bn onto the sector, according to the trade body.
The Consortium has urged Healey to push the NICs threshold back up to £6,000 at next month’s Budget to encourage retailers to hire more young people.
The government has faced huge pressure in recent months to tackle the crisis of youth unemployment. Nearly 1m young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training (Neet).
“The Chancellor can turn the tide on unemployment and tackle the Neets crisis that is robbing a generation of young people of opportunity,” said BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson.
Healey urged to slash retail taxes
The retail sector has shed 115,000 jobs in the past two years, according to the trade body’s research, which found that nearly a quarter of young people get their first jobs in the sector.
Dickinson added: “Retail has always been one of the great gateways into work, giving millions of people their first job and the skills and confidence to build a career.
“Previous changes to NICs hit retail disproportionately hard and soaring employment costs are making it harder for retailers to offer the crucial entry-level roles that so many young people rely on.”
Retailers are also bracing for the government’s incoming crackdown on zero-hour contracts. Lord Wolfson, the boss of Next, has warned that these new rules will make it “much harder” for the retail giant to offer more hours to its staff.
The BRC’s letter also called on Healey to slash taxes to encourage investment in the UK’s economy. The Chancellor should cut retailers’ energy bills and exempt all shops from the high-value business rates multiplier, the group said.
On Tuesday, a group of retailers including Primark, Morrisons and Tesco told Andy Burnham to rule out a hike to the business rates multiplier facing large high street companies.
The Prime Minister has committed to easing the business rates burden facing pubs and hotels, and the Retail Jobs Alliance warned that retail stores are “integral to high street renaissance”.
Bunrham and Healey have refused to be drawn on any major fiscal plans and have insisted they will set out more details at the Budget.

items.title: Tesco, B&Q and Whitbread scolded in minimum wage crackdown
items.summary: Labour’s new workers’ rights police force has scolded Tesco, B&Q and Whitbread, and more than 600 other firms, for failing to pay the minimum wage.  The Fair Work Agency has published the names of 658 companies which have been fined £7m and forced to return £4m to more than 27,000 workers who have not been [...]
items.body:
Tesco, B&Q and Whitbread scolded in minimum wage crackdown
Labour’s new workers’ rights police force has scolded Tesco, B&Q and Whitbread, and more than 600 other firms, for failing to pay the minimum wage.
The Fair Work Agency has published the names of 658 companies which have been fined £7m and forced to return £4m to more than 27,000 workers who have not been paid the legal rate.
Announcing the crackdown, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: “Short-changing your staff isn’t a shortcut to success, and we are determined to stamp it out.”
Tesco was among the businesses singled out by the new workers’ rights police, after the grocer failed to pay £227.84 to one worker.
Home improvement retailer B&Q, which is owned by FTSE-100-listed Kingfisher, was ordered to pay back nearly £457,000 to 4,530 workers who the government said have not been paid the minimum wage.
Whitbread, the FTSE 100 hospitality firm which owns Premier Inn, failed to pay nearly £4,200 to 342 employees, the Fair Work Agency said.
Two franchises of burger titan McDonald’s, based in Essex and Warwickshire, were made to pay back more than £29,000 to 797 workers in total.
Outsourcing giant Serco, fast-food chain Five Guys and private security firm G4S were also named among the companies which failed to pay minimum wage.
Workers’ rights police flexes muscles
Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: “Underpaying your staff is illegal, and we will not let workers foot the bill for their boss failing to follow the rules.
“We’re making sure workers get the hard-earned pay they deserve, and where employers fall short, they will be held to account.”
The Fair Work Agency was set up in April under the Employment Rights Act and has been given new powers to ensure companies pay the minimum wage and comply with the government’s new workers’ rights clampdown.
The agency has powers to search individuals and work premises, and seize evidence if it suspects a firm has fallen foul of employment law.
Matthew Taylor, chair of the agency’s advisory board, said: “This naming round is an important reminder that paying the minimum wage is not optional — it is the law.
“Most employers want to do the right thing, and we will support them to comply, but those who fall short should expect robust enforcement to protect workers and maintain a fair playing field for responsible businesses.”
A spokesperson for B&Q said its minimum wage shortfalls were unintentional, adding that the affected workers were paid in full in July last year. A Tesco spokesperson said it was “sorry” for an “isolated administrative error”. They added: “This was quickly resolved and we have taken steps to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
A Serco spokesperson said: “A technical error affected one contract more than two years ago and related to salary sacrifice schemes. It was quickly rectified once identified and all employees were reimbursed in full.”
The McDonald’s franchisees apologised to all affected employees and took steps to resolve the pay issues as soon as they were made aware of them, a spokesperson for the company said.

items.title: Retailers urge John Healey to undo Reeves's High Street tax raid and 'turn the tide' on job cuts
items.summary: The British Retail Consortium has written to the new Chancellor to ask him to raise the threshold at which employers pay their staff's NI contributions.
items.body:
Retailers urge John Healey to undo Reeves's High Street tax raid and 'turn the tide' on job cuts
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
High Street retailers have urged John Healey to roll back Rachel Reeves’ employer National Insurance raid to ‘turn the tide’ on unemployment.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC) estimates that the policy has, together with rises in minimum wages, cost the sector £6.5billion and 115,000 jobs.
Reeves’ raid, announced in 2024, saw the annual salary threshold at which NICs must be paid by employers cut from £9,100 to £5,000. The change in April 2025 also saw the NICs rate rise from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent.
The High Street reeled as employers were liable to pay the tax on many more workers, including young people employed on a part-time basis.
The BRC estimates the threshold change cost £1.74billion.
Now, the trade body, which represents major retailers, including Sainsbury’s and Tesco, has written to the Chancellor to ask him to raise the threshold to £6,000 to help firms hire more as it would undo some damage.
Retail jobs: The British Retail Consortium has written to the new Chancellor to ask him to raise the threshold at which employers pay their staff’s NI contributions
As the country battles a ‘crisis’ of young people who are not ‘earning or learning’, BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said the sector ‘is uniquely placed to play a central role’.
Businesses are issuing pleas ahead of the Budget in October after the Government said it was ‘committed to restoring high streets and bringing back hope across Britain’.
Dickinson said that thriving shopping streets are ‘essential to achieving stronger growth and raising living standards’, but firms have been held back.
Higher employment costs, energy bills, packaging taxes and business rates have ‘reduced the industry’s capacity to invest, create opportunities for young people and support growth’, she said.
The October 28 Budget could be a ‘turning point’ to ‘help deliver Government’s missions on growth, jobs and thriving high streets’.
Retailers also want the Government to act on the extra levies on energy bills and to ease business rates increases.
Meanwhile, the Association of Convenience Stores urged the Government to ‘keep the cost of employment under control and ensure workplace reforms support, rather than limit, job creation’.
Retailers are concerned that workers’ rights reforms will mean more red tape and administrative costs that make it harder to employ staff on a flexible basis, including students and Christmas temporary workers.

items.title: Why are modern consumers comfortably spending more time on digital platforms than high street shops?

Once upon a time, the great British High Street was king. Online shopping? That was the alternative. Consumers would check out the wares and stock of a high street store first, then head to its website to order any unavailable or elusive items. Six years ago, the pandemic upended that hierarchy. Shops closed, and eCommerce […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Once upon a time, the great British High Street was king. Online shopping? That was the alternative. Consumers would check out the wares and stock of a high street store first, then head to its website to order any unavailable or elusive items.
Six years ago, the pandemic upended that hierarchy. Shops closed, and eCommerce became essential. Yet, the reopening of the high street did little to restore the old order. If anything, consecutive lockdowns accelerated a behavioural shift that was already well underway.
As a result, modern consumers aren’t just living through the rise of digital retail, but are existing in a new ecosystem in which digital is the default environment for much of everyday life. So, how did we get here?
A pandemic spike became a permanent shift
There’s plenty of figures to bear this out. For instance, according to the Office for National Statistics, internet sales accounted for just 7.1% of British retail in 2010. That share reached 21.6% by 2019, then surged to 37.8% in 2021. Crucially, high street spending never returned to its pre-pandemic level, with online sales still representing 27.4% of all retail spending to date.
Meanwhile, BRC-Sensormatic data shows that UK footfall fell by another 0.8% in 2025, marking its third consecutive annual decline. Shopping centres were hit particularly hard during December, when visitor numbers dropped by 5.1% year on year.
That impact can be felt. Fashion retailers and department stores haven’t just had to contend with reduced footfall: return rates are higher than ever, while shoppers can now compare dozens of competitively priced alternatives before entering a fitting room. Conversely, ecommerce logistics, food delivery, streaming subscriptions and app-based leisure have expanded around consumers who now expect services to come to them.
Convenience is just the beginning
The obvious advantage of a digital platform is that it never closes. A shopper can simply replace that broken kettle during their commute or order groceries at midnight. But convenience alone doesn’t explain why Britons continue to remain online long after the purchase has been made…
Digital platforms condense several stages of the buying journey into one place. Discovery, price comparison, payment and customer feedback can all happen within a matter of minutes. The shift echoes well beyond eCommerce and stretches into how consumers choose to occupy their downtime.
Cinemas have a limited number of screens, but Netflix is content on demand. A local casino’s game offering is limited by floor space, but a comparison site means customers can compare licensed UK operators to read up on games, bonuses or payment options before choosing where to wager. In each case, digital platforms expand choice by removing many of the physical limitations that shape traditional leisure activities.
These advantages are felt by businesses and consumers alike. Digital access has allowed shopping and leisure to occupy moments that were previously commercially inactive, offering greater choice while removing the barriers of distance and fixed trading hours. Even when something is out of stock, an alternative is typically just another tab away.
Social media’s rewritten the customer journey
There’s also a real era-specific reason why the high street’s losing out to the online realm. Social media is ubiquitous, precisely because digital platforms are where culture now happens.
Say a shopper encounters a skincare product in a TikTok tutorial; they can read feedback instantly and even complete the purchase without leaving the app. It’s not about “going shopping” anymore. Inspiration and transaction have begun to merge.
Algorithms then make this environment feel tailored and personal. A shop presents the same displays to everyone who enters on a given day, but social media feeds re-organise themselves around each user. The feed feels relevant, immediate…it’s almost like the right product has found the consumer, rather than the other way around.
Physical retail still has a card up its sleeve
What does all this mean for the future of the high street in the UK? An obvious answer is that eCommerce businesses will continue to dominate, outlasting physical and even hybrid retailers. That’s not necessarily the case.
In-store shopping can be immediate in different ways to shopping on a smartphone screen. Why? Because it’s full of qualities that are simply impossible to reproduce through a tech device. Expertise, the tactile nature of browsing and selecting products, human interaction, they all add up to create a distinct experience.
What’s crucial is that retail businesses start to capitalise on this. Future-proofing a business isn’t simply about digitising everything. It involves identifying which parts of the customer journey benefit from being faster, broader or more personalised online, and which are more valuable in person.
Consumers are spending more time on digital platforms because those platforms have absorbed shopping and leisure behaviours into the wider rhythm of daily life, not because brick-and-mortar experiences don’t matter any more. The retailers who’ll hold their attention are the ones giving reasons to use both.

items.body:
Dmitry Nikolaev - stock.adobe.co
Mythos helps bug bounty firm find critical hidden RCE
HackerOne used Anthropic's controversial Claude Mythos 5 model on its codebase and found a critical hidden flaw.
Bug bounty programme operator HackerOne has revealed it has patched a dangerous remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in its production environment that it would likely never have found had it not set Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 frontier artificial intelligence (AI) model on its codebase.
HackerOne signed up to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing – a defensive cyber initiative established to give trusted third-parties access to Claude Mythos 5 – in order to run a series of sandboxed experiments.
According to HackerOne chief product officer Nidhi Aggarwal, Mythos surfaced the critical, no production exposure flaw in its first run against the firm’s codebase. She said that while deployment conditions prevented it from being publicly exploitable, had a specific change been made it could have become reachable.
“The interesting part wasn't the finding itself. It was how the vulnerability got there,” wrote Aggarwal. “The RCE came from three individually safe code changes.”
The first of these changes was a dynamic method dispatch protected by a GraphQL schema enum. The second was a new analytics version that introduced an untyped filter argument. The third was a refactor that consolidated the two. In context, these changes would have been relatively harmless. However, when all three changes were in production at the same time, they combined to create the RCE flaw.
“We think about this as compositional risk: vulnerabilities that don't live in any single commit, but in how safe-in-isolation changes interact over time,” Aggarwal explained in a technical write-up detailing the discovery.
“Traditional code review evaluates pull requests in isolation; it's structurally blind to this class of problem. Whole-program static analysis had a better chance of finding something like this, since it reasons over the entire tree rather than one diff at a time. But these tools struggle to model custom sinks, and often cannot resolve dynamic dispatch.”
Mythos, she said, had proven adept at following trails across various commits and authors until it found the loose thread where the logic had come apart.
Aggarwal stressed that the core problem of accumulating implicit assumptions across subsystems, authors and time was a universal one that could affect any organisation shipping code at speed. Most of the assumptions should hold, she said, but some will not, and those that do not won’t be easily spotted. Mythos, she suggested, holds value in that it can reason across these accumulations to find such problems.
Having resolved the RCE flaw, HackerOne ran a series of follow-on experiments from which it has drawn three core conclusions:
- Firstly, that AI models are not just finding more vulnerabilities, but more sophisticated ones;
- Secondly, that validating and confirming these flaws is going to become a dangerous bottleneck, with Mythos generating new findings faster than humans can triage them – new approaches to validation and remediation will be needed;
- Thirdly, that the harnesses and guardrails used to control models like Mythos also need to change to reflect the need to review what it finds and how those findings are put across.
Read more about AI for vulnerability discovery
- AI platforms are poised to accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation faster than humans can manage. It's time for CISOs to rethink their security strategies.
- AI accelerates exploit timelines from months to hours. Organisations must shift from patch-all to risk-based prioritisation using exploitability metrics.
- Enterprises are working out how to give AI agents identities of their own, says Ping Identity CEO Andre Durand, just as frontier models start finding vulnerabilities faster than anyone can patch them.

Asda has completed the rollout of 1.2 million ESELs into all… This story continues at Asda rolls out digital shelf labels across all Express convenience stores Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The electronic labels will replace the manual task of swapping over 120,000 paper price tickets each week.
Asda has completed the rollout of 1.2 million ESELs into all of its 517 Asda Express stores.
The retailer said the change would mean staff “can better use their time to serve customers, improve availability and maintain store standards”.
Matt Harrison, director of central operations at Asda Express, said: “By removing manual pricing tasks, we’re freeing up time for colleagues to focus on serving customers and keeping store standards high. It’s another example of how we’re modernising our stores to improve the shopping experience for customers.”
